newsitem.title: UK: Asian LPG interest starts to emerge, Europe steady.
newsitem.headline: Asian LPG interest starts to emerge, Europe steady.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) markets saw good interest from parts of Europe and the Americas this week, traders said, although Japanese and South Korean buyers are still hoping for lower prices in the summer, keeping East Asian demand relatively muted.

Japan and Korea traditionally buy large spot volumes during the summer, when prices are at their lowest, to build up stocks ahead of the period of peak demand in the winter. But this has not yet started in earnest, a trader said, as buyers still expect prices to fall.
"Japan and Korea need not be in a hurry," he said. "It's now getting warmer, so there is no need to build up stocks. There's plenty of time, so it's a matter of the price level."

Players are waiting for the publication of Saudi Aramco's Contract Price (CP), the benchmark against which most LPG in Asian markets is traded. The CP takes into consideration three spot tenders issued every month.

Although the details of the most recent tenders have not been confirmed, rumours suggest that for propane, T1 was awarded at around $165 a tonne fob Gulf, T2 at around $170 a tonne, and T3 at between $165 and $170 a tonne.
But one source said that the T3 was thought to have been awarded below $160 a tonne. Even so, this apparent weakening was not expected to have a major effect on bringing down the May CP.
Several dealers said they anticipated the propane price in May to be set at around $175 a tonne, and estimates for the butane level varied between $5 and $15 a tonne above the propane price.
These levels may not yet be low enough to lure Japanese buyers back into the market, a trader said.
"Prices are getting better but they're not yet good enough," said a Japanese trader. "The Japanese expect a low price."
He also pointed out that even if the CP falls, spot premiums to the benchmark may yet rise, which could still have the effect of keeping buyers sidelined.
The trader also speculated that as the CP comes down, there may be more funds available to allow China to enter the spot market as a big buyer in the summer.

Dealers expect Asian spot activity to increase soon as the summer progresses. The Middle East Gulf market is still reasonably quiet on a spot basis, a dealer said, but interest is picking up. "It's not very active in the Gulf, but buyers are starting to sniff around."

In Europe, the main driver for propane prices was demand for small sea-going coasters for delivery to Portugal. Prices continue firm, with a two-tier market in place depending on whether material meets the Portuguese specification or not. For Portuguese spec, a dealer said prices were in the range $185 to $190 a tonne fob NWE, while for material which does not meet the spec, there was a discount of up to $20 a tonne.

"There's still quite healthy activity with a number of requests coming in," he said. He added that butane coasters were languishing with little demand seen, and the market is well supplied. Butane coasters are valued in the high $130's a tonne, he said, increasing to the low or mid $140's for the right quality or if the material is co-loaded with propane.

On the large cargo market in Europe, a propane trade at $186 a month cif NWE for end April delivery is seen as unrepeatable, with even sellers agreeing that the next trade is likely to be done in the mid $170's a tonne. The seller of that large cargo also sold a seagoing coaster at $190 fob Scandinavia, and he believed the market had been relatively busy.

"On the whole the market's been quite active, with a bit going on behind the scenes," he said. "The U.S. is looking perky, it's strong enough to keep Algerian cargoes out of the North Sea, and long may it continue," he added.

Another trader pointed out that Mont Belvieu, Texas propane prices at around 35 cents a gallon or above equate to around $182 dollars a tonne. And with freight for large vessels at between $10 and $15 a tonne this nets back to around $170 a tonne fob Algeria, making trans-Atlantic sales the most attractive option now for Mediterranean sellers.

Small propane cargoes were valued at $180/$185 a tonne cif Lavera in southern France, and although large cargoes were notionally at a discount to this, the difficulty of finding storage space for such cargoes in the summer was keeping the market thin. Butane was discussed in the $160's a tonne cif Lavera but the market was extremely illiquid.
